intro: Searching for a physio usually means something is hurting, stiff or not working the way it used to, and you want help from someone who understands movement and muscles. Perhaps you have a bad back, a sports injury, a joint that has been operated on, or a condition that affects how you walk or use your hands. Whatever has prompted your search, it helps to know what a physiotherapist does and what to have ready when you get in touch.
need_heading: What people searching for a physio usually need
need_lead: Most enquiries about a physio come from people dealing with pain, recovery or movement problems that are getting in the way of everyday life.
needs: You have back, neck or shoulder pain that has lingered and you want it properly assessed rather than just eased for an hour.
You are recovering from a sports injury and need help getting back to running, lifting or playing the way you did before.
You have had surgery on a joint or a ligament and need rehabilitation to build strength and movement again.
You have a neurological condition such as a stroke or Parkinson's and want support with balance, walking or using your hands.
You are stiff after an accident, a fall or a long spell of inactivity and want a plan of exercises to get moving again.
context: "Physiotherapist" and "physical therapist" are protected titles in the UK. Anyone using them must be registered with the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC), and you can check the HCPC register online. Most physiotherapists are also members of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy (CSP), shown by the letters MCSP.

Sports therapists, massage therapists and personal trainers can be helpful for some needs, but they are not physiotherapists. For an injury, post-surgery rehabilitation or a neurological condition, check that you are booking an HCPC-registered physiotherapist.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the problem in your own words, such as where it hurts and how long it has been going on.
Say what you think caused it, whether that was an injury, an operation, an illness or simply something that came on gradually.
Mention any diagnosis or treatment you have already had, including scans, hospital appointments or previous physiotherapy.
Explain what you are struggling with day to day, such as walking, sleeping, lifting, driving or getting dressed.
Say whether you would prefer to be seen at a clinic or at home, and give the area you live in so we can introduce you to someone local.
Mention any condition or medication that might affect your treatment, so the professional can plan around it.
questions: Are you registered with the HCPC, and what is your registration number?
How many sessions do you think I might need, and how will we judge whether it is working?
Will you give me exercises to do at home between appointments?
What should I wear or bring to the first appointment?
Do you have experience of treating my particular problem or condition?
What will the assessment involve, and how will you explain the plan to me?

faqs.a: "Physio" is short for physiotherapy or physiotherapist. It is the assessment and treatment of muscles, joints and movement to reduce pain and restore function, and it is carried out by an HCPC-registered physiotherapist.

faqs.q: What happens at a first physiotherapy appointment?
faqs.a: The first session usually includes an assessment of your problem, your movement and your history. The physiotherapist will then explain what they think is going on and agree a plan with you, which often includes exercises to do at home.

faqs.q: What should I bring and wear?
faqs.a: Wear comfortable clothing you can move in, and bring anything relevant such as a list of your medication, scan results or letters from a hospital. If your problem is with a knee or shoulder, loose clothing that lets the area be examined is helpful.

faqs.q: Can a sports therapist or massage therapist help instead?
faqs.a: They can be helpful for some needs, but they are not physiotherapists. For an injury, post-surgery rehabilitation or a neurological condition, check that you are booking an HCPC-registered physiotherapist.

extra: Because "physio" is such a short, everyday word, people often use it loosely for anything from a sports massage to a full rehabilitation programme. It is worth being clear with yourself about what you actually want: a one-off assessment of a nagging problem, ongoing treatment after an operation, or help managing a long-term condition. That clarity will shape the questions you ask and the kind of professional you feel comfortable with.

Physiotherapy tends to work best when you are an active participant rather than a passive recipient. Much of the progress happens between appointments through the exercises you are given, so ask how to do them correctly, how often to practise and what to do if something flares up. If a particular exercise makes things worse, say so at the next session rather than quietly abandoning it.

It also helps to think about how you will judge progress. Pain can ease before strength and movement return, or the other way round, so ask the physiotherapist what changes they will be looking for and over what sort of period. Being able to describe your day-to-day function, such as whether you can climb stairs or carry shopping, gives you a practical measure alongside how you feel.

extra_faqs.q: Can I see a physiotherapist without a referral from my GP?
extra_faqs.a: Yes, in the UK you can usually contact a physiotherapist directly without seeing your GP first. Some clinics ask for a brief history when you book, and if your problem turns out to need medical investigation they will advise you to see your GP.

No. Physiotherapists also help with long-term conditions, recovery after surgery, balance problems and movement difficulties linked to neurological conditions. The common thread is helping you move and function better, whatever the underlying cause.

extra_faqs.q: What if the physiotherapist thinks I need something else?
extra_faqs.a: A good physiotherapist will tell you if your problem is outside what they can help with and suggest the right next step, such as seeing your GP. That is a sign of good practice rather than a reason to worry.
